title: Chemistry Foundations
summary: Learn the foundations of chemistry with worked calculations: atoms, elements and isotopes, the periodic table, chemical bonding, reactions and balancing equations, moles and concentration, and acids, bases and everyday safe chemistry.
audience: Secondary students, adult learners, health and agriculture students, and anyone curious about chemistry

body.p: Chemistry studies matter: what substances are made of, how they behave and how they change. All matter is made of atoms, and an element is a substance made of only one kind of atom. There are 118 known elements.

list: Protons: positive charge, in the nucleus. The number of protons is the atomic number and defines the element.
Neutrons: no charge, in the nucleus.
Electrons: negative charge, very light, arranged in shells around the nucleus.
Mass number = protons + neutrons. Sodium has 11 protons and usually 12 neutrons, so its mass number is 23.
A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons.

body.p: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. Chlorine has two common isotopes, chlorine-35 (about 75.8%) and chlorine-37 (about 24.2%), so its average relative atomic mass is about 34.97 x 0.7578 + 36.97 x 0.2422, which is 35.45.

body.tip: Learn the symbols of the first 20 elements; they appear in most beginner chemistry.

body.p: The periodic table arranges elements in order of atomic number so that elements with similar properties fall in the same column.

list: Groups (columns) contain elements with the same number of outer-shell electrons, so they react similarly. Group 1 (alkali metals such as sodium) react vigorously with water; Group 18 (noble gases) are very unreactive.
Periods (rows) show the number of electron shells.
Electron arrangement: sodium (11 electrons) is 2, 8, 1; chlorine (17 electrons) is 2, 8, 7.
Metals are on the left and centre; non-metals on the right; metalloids such as silicon lie between.

body.p: Reactivity of metals increases down Group 1 because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and lost more easily. Reactivity of halogens (Group 17) decreases down the group. Such patterns let chemists predict properties of elements they have not studied.

body.tip: Use the group number to predict the charge of simple ions: Group 1 forms 1+ ions, Group 2 forms 2+, Group 17 forms 1- ions.

body.p: Atoms bond to achieve stable electron arrangements, often a full outer shell.

list: Ionic bonding: metals transfer electrons to non-metals, forming oppositely charged ions held together strongly. Sodium chloride (table salt) is Na⁺ and Cl⁻ in a giant lattice. Ionic compounds have high melting points and conduct electricity when melted or dissolved.
Covalent bonding: non-metals share pairs of electrons. Water (H₂O) has two O-H bonds; carbon dioxide (CO₂) has two C=O double bonds. Simple covalent substances often have low melting points.
Metallic bonding: metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, explaining why metals conduct electricity and can be shaped.
Giant covalent structures, such as diamond and silicon dioxide (sand), are very hard with high melting points.

body.p: Structure explains properties: graphite conducts electricity and is slippery because its layers have free electrons and slide over each other, while diamond, made of the same carbon atoms, is the hardest natural substance.

body.tip: Ask "metal plus non-metal?" (usually ionic) or "non-metals only?" (usually covalent) to predict bonding.

body.p: In a chemical reaction, atoms rearrange to form new substances. Signs include colour change, gas bubbles, a precipitate (solid forming), and energy given out or taken in.

Atoms are neither created nor destroyed, so equations must balance. Hydrogen burns in oxygen to form water: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Count: 4 hydrogen atoms and 2 oxygen atoms on each side. This conservation of mass means the total mass of products equals the total mass of reactants.

list: Combustion: fuels react with oxygen, releasing energy: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.
Neutralisation: acid + base → salt + water.
Displacement: a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from a compound.
Decomposition: one substance breaks into simpler ones, such as limestone into lime and carbon dioxide when heated.
Oxidation and reduction (redox): rusting of iron is oxidation.

body.p: Exothermic reactions release heat (burning); endothermic reactions absorb heat (photosynthesis, cold packs).

body.tip: Balance equations by changing the numbers in front of formulas, never the small subscript numbers.

body.p: Chemists count particles by weighing. One mole contains about 6.022 x 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number), and the mass of one mole in grams equals the relative formula mass.

list: Water (H₂O): 2 x 1.008 + 16.00 = 18.02 g/mol. 36 g of water is 36 / 18.02, about 2.00 mol, containing about 1.20 x 10²⁴ molecules.
Carbon dioxide (CO₂): 12.01 + 2 x 16.00 = 44.01 g/mol.
Sodium chloride (NaCl): 22.99 + 35.45 = 58.44 g/mol.
Moles = mass / molar mass.

body.p: Concentration (mol/L) = moles / volume in litres. Dissolving 5.85 g of NaCl (about 0.100 mol) in water to make 0.5 L of solution gives about 0.20 mol/L. Concentration calculations are used in medicine, agriculture (fertiliser solutions) and industry.

body.tip: Always write units at every step: g, g/mol, mol, L. Units reveal mistakes.

body.p: Acids produce hydrogen ions (H⁺) in water; bases neutralise acids, and soluble bases (alkalis) produce hydroxide ions (OH⁻).

list: pH runs from about 0 to 14: below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral (pure water), above 7 is alkaline.
Each step of 1 is a tenfold change: pH 3 is 10² = 100 times more acidic than pH 5.
Examples: stomach acid about 1 to 2, lemon juice about 2, rain about 5.6, blood about 7.4, soap and baking soda solutions alkaline.
Indicators such as litmus, universal indicator, or red cabbage juice show pH by colour.

body.p: Farmers add lime to neutralise acidic soils; antacids neutralise excess stomach acid; soaps and detergents remove grease; water treatment uses chemistry to make water safe. Laboratory and household safety matters: wear eye protection, never mix bleach with acids or ammonia (it releases toxic gases), add acid to water rather than water to acid, and read hazard labels.

body.tip: Test the pH of household substances safely with red cabbage indicator; it is a simple home experiment.
